title: Fossil CEO Announces Accelerated Turnaround as Sales Surge Back into Growth, CNBC Reports
body:
Fossil Group Inc. reported a modest but encouraging rebound in its quarterly earnings, signaling that the company’s multi‑year turnaround plan may be gaining traction earlier than expected. The watchmaker posted a return to profitability and a slight uptick in revenue, marking the first instance of sales growth in several quarters after years of declining demand from both traditional retailers and digital competitors.

The 2024 second‑quarter results showed net income of $12.6 million, a reversal from a loss of $28 million a year earlier, while revenue climbed 3.2 percent to $1.01 billion. The improvement was driven primarily by a resurgence in the United States and Europe, where Fossil’s “modern classic” collections resonated with consumers seeking affordable yet stylish accessories. In addition, the company’s licensing agreements with fashion houses such as Michael Kors and Diesel contributed a modest boost, as those partners rolled out new hybrid smartwatch models that blend analog aesthetics with limited digital functionality.

Analysts attribute the modest recovery to several strategic pivots the firm has undertaken since 2022. First, Fossil has shifted focus away from low‑margin, mass‑market timepieces toward higher‑margin, fashion‑forward designs that command premium pricing. The company also streamlined its supply chain, consolidating production in fewer facilities and renegotiating terms with key component suppliers, which reduced cost of goods sold by roughly 4 percent year‑over‑year. Moreover, Fossil has embraced a “smart‑watch lite” approach, integrating basic fitness tracking and notification features into its analog‑styled watches without the full hardware expense of competing wearable brands. This hybrid model has appealed to older consumers who prefer a traditional look but still want limited connectivity.

Despite the positive signs, the path ahead remains fraught with challenges. The broader watch industry continues to grapple with the rise of smartphones and dedicated wearables, which have eroded the relevance of traditional timepieces. Fossil’s reliance on licensing deals also introduces uncertainty, as partner brands may alter their strategic priorities or launch competing products. Furthermore, inventory levels remain elevated in certain regions, prompting the company to offer deeper discounts that could compress margins if sales do not sustain. Investors are watching closely for the company’s ability to convert early momentum into consistent top‑line growth and to maintain profitability without resorting to aggressive price cuts.

The firm’s management remains optimistic, projecting a 5‑to‑7 percent revenue increase for the full fiscal year and targeting a 10‑percent operating margin by 2026. To achieve these goals, Fossil plans to expand its e‑commerce footprint, leveraging data‑driven marketing to reach younger demographics while preserving its heritage appeal. The company also announced a partnership with a major Chinese technology provider to develop a next‑generation hybrid smartwatch that could bridge the gap between fashion and function, potentially opening new channels in the fast‑growing Asian market.

If Fossil can sustain its nascent sales growth and continue to refine its product mix, the turnaround could evolve from a brief resurgence into a durable revival. The coming quarters will be critical in confirming whether the early gains are the result of a lasting strategic shift or a temporary lift from seasonal factors. Stakeholders will be watching not only the numbers but also how effectively Fossil can navigate the evolving consumer preferences that have reshaped the watch industry over the past decade.
